checkpoints: Nêu nguyên tắc bao trùm là least privilege / giảm blast-radius: giả định kẻ tấn công có RCE sẽ chạy lệnh tuỳ ý dưới danh nghĩa (identity) của worker, nên identity đó phải đọc/ghi được càng ít càng tốt.
Identity: chạy service dưới một service account riêng, non-login (vd `useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin appworker`) với group riêng của nó — không dùng root, không dùng chung với service khác.

Code files: chủ sở hữu là một deploy identity khác, group `appworker`, quyền `750`/`640` — service chỉ đọc/thực thi được chứ KHÔNG ghi được chính code của nó, để dù bị RCE kẻ tấn công cũng không thể sửa code để persist.

Config files quyền `640`, owner root, group `appworker` (nhóm `other` không có quyền gì); log directory quyền `750`, owned by `appworker` để service ghi log được — khác biệt cốt lõi: config chỉ đọc, log phải ghi được.

Secret files: quyền `600` (hoặc `640` owner root/group `appworker`), tuyệt đối không cho `other`; tốt hơn nữa nên dùng cơ chế credential của systemd (`LoadCredential=`) để secret không rải rác trên filesystem.
UMask trong unit systemd: đặt `UMask=0027` trong `[Service]` (không phải trong `.bashrc` vì service không load shell profile) để mọi file worker tạo ra mặc định `640`/`750`, không lộ cho `other`.
Hardening bổ sung ở unit systemd: `NoNewPrivileges=yes`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, `PrivateTmp=yes`, `ReadOnlyPaths=` để RCE không leo thang quyền hay ghi ra ngoài phạm vi cho phép.

Bác bỏ đề xuất setuid: sai ở hai điểm — kernel Linux CỐ TÌNH bỏ qua bit setuid/setgid trên script thông dịch (`#!/usr/bin/python3`) nên nó không có tác dụng gì; và kể cả với ELF binary, setuid lại NÂNG quyền tiến trình, đi ngược mục tiêu thu hẹp blast-radius — nếu cần một hành động đặc quyền cụ thể thì cấp sudo NOPASSWD cho đúng lệnh đó hoặc một Linux capability có mục tiêu, chứ không dùng setuid tràn lan.

"Connection refused" means the SYN reached the host and the OS replied with RST — points to a service/socket-layer problem (nothing listening, or a firewall REJECT rule), investigated on the server itself.

"Connection timed out" means the SYN was dropped with no reply — points to a network/firewall-layer problem (firewall DENY, black-hole route, security group, or a dead host), investigated along the network path.
Root cause: service not listening or crashed — confirm with `ss -tlnp` (optionally `ss -tlnp 'sport = :PORT'`) plus `systemctl status <svc>`; this shows up to the client as refused.

Root cause: service bound to `127.0.0.1` instead of `0.0.0.0` — confirm because `curl 127.0.0.1:PORT` on the box succeeds while external calls are refused, and the Local Address column in `ss -tlnp` shows the loopback bind.

Root cause: firewall or cloud security group blocking the port — confirm via `ufw status` / `iptables -L -n` on the host and the cloud security group config; the port shows as listening in `ss` yet external connections time out (dropped).

Fast bisection / inside-out technique: run `curl 127.0.0.1:PORT` from the server itself first — success means the service is fine and the bug is bind-address or firewall/network related (look outward), while a local refusal means the service itself isn't listening (look at the service) — this stops you misdiagnosing the layer by blaming the network before confirming the service came up.
Mechanism: dùng SSH public-key authentication thay cho shared root password — private key nằm trên client và KHÔNG BAO GIỜ đi qua mạng, public key nằm trong `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` trên server.

Giải thích ở tầng handshake: server gửi 1 challenge ngẫu nhiên, client ký challenge đó bằng private key rồi gửi lại chữ ký, server verify bằng public key — không có password nào đi qua đường truyền (kể cả đã mã hoá) nên không thể phish/brute-force từ xa, và Ed25519 key có entropy rất cao.

Audit "who did what" sau khi bỏ shared root: mỗi engineer có account riêng + public key riêng (không còn shared root), mọi hành động privileged đi qua sudo và được log vào `/var/log/auth.log` kèm username thật + command thực thi.

Các dòng cần đổi trong `sshd_config`: `PasswordAuthentication no`, `PermitRootLogin no` (hoặc `prohibit-password`), `PubkeyAuthentication yes`, và tuỳ chọn `AllowGroups ssh-users` để giới hạn ai được login.

Thứ tự bật firewall trên MỘT host để không tự khoá mình: allow port 22 (`ufw allow 22/tcp` / `ufw allow OpenSSH`) TRƯỚC, rồi mới `ufw --force enable` (default-deny inbound); khi test rule mới luôn giữ 1 SSH session đang mở và mở thêm session thứ hai để test, kèm dead-man's switch (`at now + 5 minutes <<< 'ufw disable'`) hoặc cloud serial console làm phương án dự phòng.

Trình tự cutover trên mỗi host: phân phối public key qua config management → xác nhận mỗi engineer key-login được trên host đó → CHỈ SAU ĐÓ mới flip `PasswordAuthentication no` + `PermitRootLogin no` trong sshd_config → `systemctl reload sshd` (vẫn giữ session SSH cũ đang mở) → mới bật ufw.

Chiến lược rollout trên CẢ CLUSTER (chục server): làm kiểu canary — từng host một, verify xong mới sang host kế; TUYỆT ĐỐI không flip config/firewall trên tất cả server cùng lúc, để không tự khoá mình ra khỏi toàn bộ cluster cùng lúc.
Identifies the core distinction as declarative (Terraform only declares the desired end state) vs imperative (a bash script scripts each API call step by step).
States that with the imperative bash approach you must manually work out the correct creation order and track intermediate state yourself as the script runs.
States that with the imperative bash approach you must also hand-write your own cleanup/rollback logic for when something fails partway through.
Explains that Terraform automatically infers the correct creation order by building a dependency graph from references between resources (e.g. a subnet pointing to its VPC id).
Explains Terraform's reconciliation loop: it compares the declared desired state against the current real-world state and applies only the difference needed to close the gap.
Identifies terraform.tfstate as the JSON file recording the mapping between resources declared in code and the real-world resources actually created (their ids/attributes).
States that if the state file is deleted, Terraform loses track of what already exists, so the next apply will attempt to recreate the resources from scratch.

Gives a concrete consequence of that recreation attempt — e.g. wasteful duplicate resources (double cost) when duplicate names are allowed, or an 'already exists' error forcing a manual terraform import when names must be unique.
Disagree with the suggestion to drop version pinning — dropping the pin is exactly how you get "works on my machine, fails in CI".

The `~>` (pessimistic constraint) operator only allows the rightmost component to increase: `~> 3.6` (2 components) means `>= 3.6.0, < 4.0.0` (minor/patch allowed, major blocked); `~> 3.6.2` (3 components) means `>= 3.6.2, < 3.7.0` (only patch allowed, stricter).

Without a pinned version and/or without `.terraform.lock.hcl`, every `init` resolves to whatever is the latest version matching the registry at that exact moment — resolution is non-deterministic across time.

Because resolution depends on the moment `init` runs, 3 people plus CI running `init` at 3 different points in time can pull 3 different provider versions, causing diverging behavior even though the `.tf` code is identical.
The right approach includes always setting `version = "~> x.y"` in `required_providers`.

The right approach also requires committing `.terraform.lock.hcl` — it records the version, constraints, and hashes (SHA256, both `h1:` and `zh:`) that were resolved, so everyone and CI init to the exact same version and checksum.

`terraform init -upgrade` is the only command allowed to actively bypass the lock and re-resolve to a newer version; without that flag, `init` always reuses the version pinned in the lock even if `.tf` changed the constraint.

CI should run `terraform init -lockfile=readonly` so the build fails immediately if `.tf` changes a constraint without the lock having been updated via `-upgrade`, instead of silently drifting versions.
Đúng: request nào tới S3 trước sẽ thắng — cuộc đua được phân giải ở tầng network theo THỨ TỰ ĐẾN của request PutObject, không phải theo tính đồng thời tuyệt đối.
Đúng: cơ chế lock của Terraform là tạo một object `<key>.tflock` trong S3 bucket để đại diện cho lock.
Đúng: request PutObject tạo lock dùng CONDITIONAL WRITE với header `If-None-Match: *` — chỉ thành công nếu object `.tflock` đó CHƯA tồn tại.
Đúng: bên thắng (A) nhận `200 OK` trên PutObject đó và nhờ vậy giữ được lock.

Đúng: bên thua (B) nhận `412 Precondition Failed` trên cùng PutObject vì object `.tflock` đã tồn tại (do A vừa tạo) — phản hồi này là ĐỒNG BỘ/tức thời, không cần polling hay heartbeat để biết lock đang bị giữ.
Đúng: khi apply của A xong, Terraform gọi `DeleteObject` xoá `.tflock` để giải phóng lock, sau đó lần retry của B (tự động hoặc chạy lại tay) mới thành công vì object không còn tồn tại.

Đúng: KHÔNG cần bảng DynamoDB (hay coordinator ngoài) riêng vì toàn bộ tính atomic đã nằm sẵn trong guarantee conditional-write của chính S3 — không có 'bản ghi ai đang giữ lock' nào phải tạo/duy trì ở nơi khác.

Orphaned-lock clue: in the error's `Lock Info`, the `Who` field (e.g. `ci-runner-42@runner-host`) and `Created` timestamp point to the CI runner; cross-checking the CI dashboard to confirm that runner/build ended (died/timed out) long ago while the lock is still present is what tells you the lock is orphaned (nobody actually holding it).

Mechanism: `ConditionalCheckFailedException` indicates the backend uses a DynamoDB-style lock (a conditional write into a lock table); because the OOM-kill delivers SIGKILL, the process never gets to run its cleanup logic to delete the lock record, so the lock stays stuck forever even though no process is running anymore.
Correct remediation command: run `terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>` using the exact lock ID printed in the error (here `7f3a2c11-9e4d-4b8a-9c2e-1234567890ab`).
Why not manual deletion: don't manually delete the lock record in the AWS console instead — that path is prone to inconsistent operations and leaves no Terraform audit trail.

The single most important thing to confirm before running force-unlock, and the correct sequence: confirm with certainty that no other agent/CI job is actually applying against the same state (e.g. `prod/network/terraform.tfstate`) — check the CI dashboard for any other running plan/apply job and ask the team on a shared channel if needed — only once that's confirmed should you run `force-unlock`, then retry `plan`.

Why this check matters: force-unlocking at the exact moment someone is genuinely applying causes both sides to write state concurrently — precisely the race condition the lock exists to prevent — leading to state corruption or divergence.

Diagnoses this as a "God module" that bundles multiple unrelated responsibilities into one — networking (VPC/subnet), database (RDS), load balancer + compute (ALB/ECS), IAM, WAF, and DNS (Route53) — essentially the entire application stack crammed into a single module.

Identifies the input-surface problem: 34 input variables force every consumer to read and fill in nearly the whole input surface even when they only need part of it (e.g., a team that just needs a shared VPC still has to care about db_engine, lb_type, enable_waf).
Cites the guideline for an easy-to-use module — ≤10 inputs / ≤5 outputs with one clear, testable/refactorable responsibility — as the standard this module violates.

Identifies the blast-radius problem: a small change to WAF or Route53 forces plan/apply to touch every resource in the module — including the already-running RDS/VPC — increasing the risk that the change accidentally affects an unrelated infrastructure layer.

Proposes splitting the module along clear responsibility boundaries into separate modules: networking (VPC, subnet, route table), database (RDS/Aurora), compute (ECS + ALB), and security (IAM role, WAF).
Specifies that each split module should expose only the minimal output surface consumers actually need (e.g., vpc_id, subnet_ids, db_endpoint) instead of re-exposing everything.

Specifies that a root module should orchestrate by wiring one module's output into another module's input via references, giving Terraform an explicit dependency graph between modules instead of one inseparable block.

Recommends that before publishing to the internal registry each sub-module should version independently under semver, pinned via version = "~> x.y" on the consumer side, and explains why: as one giant module, even a WAF-only change forces a version bump affecting the entire registry for every team consuming it, whether they only need the VPC piece or the RDS piece.

Root cause: all 40 sub-modules independently declare the same `data "aws_ami" "app"` source, and Terraform refreshes every data source on every plan/apply — so this identical lookup executes 40 times instead of once.

Consequence: that duplicated refresh is exactly what drives the 3+ minute plan time and the occasional AMI API rate-limit hits — the cause is the per-module `data` source pattern, not the sub-module count itself.
Fix (centralize): look up the AMI once at a higher layer — the root module or a dedicated shared lookup module — and store the result in `locals` or that module's output.
Fix (propagate): each sub-module drops its own `data` source and instead receives `ami_id` through an input `variable "ami_id" {}`, so the plan makes one API call instead of 40.

Second issue: `depends_on = [data.aws_subnet.selected]` is redundant — the reference `subnet_id = data.aws_subnet.selected.id` right above it already creates an implicit dependency that Terraform infers automatically, so no manual `depends_on` is needed.
Fix: remove the redundant `depends_on` entirely — leaving it in only adds noise and misleads readers into thinking there's a hidden ordering requirement.

Verification: with `TF_LOG=DEBUG` (or counting AMI API calls), AMI requests should drop from 40 to 1, while `terraform plan` still produces the exact same resource plan as before — confirming the refactor only changed speed, not behavior.
Declares `variable "environment"` with `type = string`.
Adds a `validation` block whose `condition` uses `contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.environment)` so only those three exact values are accepted.
Sets `error_message` to a clear message that lists the valid values, so a failed validation tells the user how to fix it.
Explains the "fail-fast" name: Terraform evaluates the `validation` block at the `plan` step, before any request is sent to the cloud API.
Explains that without this validation, an invalid value would reach `apply`, where the cloud provider returns a confusing/generic error instead of pointing to `environment` as the root cause.
Notes that catching the error at `apply` instead of `plan` wastes a real apply round-trip (minutes to tens of minutes) on something `plan`-time validation could catch in seconds.
Gives a self-verification step: `terraform plan -var="environment=qa"` is blocked immediately with the exact error message, without creating any resource.
